Falcate snailfish (Careproctus cypselurus) attains a maximum recorded total length of 35 cm [Li = 35 cm], based on examination of adult specimens from the Bering Sea. This ultimate body size is relatively modest compared to some deep-dwelling liparids, but it aligns with the general scaling pattern observed in many snailfishes inhabiting cold, high-latitude waters. Juveniles during the pelagic larval phase are particularly vulnerable to predation, and their small initial size at emergence imposes constraints on early survival. Field collections indicate that the early life stages depend heavily on a high-lipid yolk reserve to sustain endotrophic development before the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding begins.

The period immediately following fertilization is critical, with incubation proceeding at a constant 3.1 °C [T = 3.1 °C] in the deep demersal environment. Under these stable thermal conditions, the yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion after 76 days [ab = 76 days] of incubation at a temperature of 3.1 °C [T = 3.1 °C]. This extended developmental duration reflects the pronounced metabolic suppression imposed by near-freezing temperatures and the relatively large egg size, which requires substantial time for complete yolk absorption. Hatching is followed by a brief lecithotrophic phase during which the protolarva relies entirely on endogenous reserves before commencing active prey capture. The transition to exogenous feeding marks a critical physiological shift, after which growth accelerates markedly.

Sexual maturity in this species is reached at a total length of 16 cm [Lp = 16 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet body mass of 62 grams [Wwp = 62 grams]. This length at puberty indicates that individuals must roughly double their mass before reproducing, investing heavily in somatic growth during the juvenile stage. Reports from trawl surveys suggest that maturation occurs relatively early relative to the species' maximum size, a pattern common among liparids inhabiting energetically constrained environments. The corresponding wet weight at puberty scales in a manner consistent with the cube-law relationship observed across many iteroparous teleosts, providing a useful benchmark for comparing life-history strategies among close relatives.

Reproductive output in Careproctus cypselurus is constrained by the cold thermal regime of its habitat. Evidence from related species indicates that under a steady ambient temperature of 3.1 °C [T = 3.1 °C], gravid females deposit approximately 1129 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1129 eggs per spawning event], with an annual spawning frequency of about 0.65 clutches per year [F_R_i = about 0.65 clutches per year]. This modest reproductive investment per unit time is characteristic of deep-water snailfishes, which produce large, yolk-laden eggs that undergo extended incubation. The trade-off between clutches per year and egg size reflects the low metabolic rates and slow developmental pace enforced by persistent near-bottom cold.

Maximum longevity in this liparid has been estimated at 10 years [am = 10 years] under natural conditions at 3.1 °C [T = 3.1 °C], based on otolith annuli counts from large adults. The hatchling wet body mass, when first emerging as a yolk-dependent prolarva, is a mere 0.0224 grams [Wwb = 0.0224 grams], placing this species among the smallest-born snailfishes relative to its eventual adult size of 650 grams [Wwi = 650 grams]. This enormous disparity between birth mass and asymptotic mass—spanning nearly five orders of magnitude—highlights the extensive post-hatching growth trajectory required to reach reproductive size. Slow aging and delayed senescence are likely adaptations to a stable but resource-poor abyssal environment where metabolic turnover is minimal.
